questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 1 \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{1+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{(1+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{1+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+s}\cdot 2s-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2s}{1+s}-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2s(1+s)-{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{s(2+s)}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(ts{e}^{t+s})(1)+({e}^{t+s})(t) \\  & =t{e}^{t+s}(s+1).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{st})^{2}}=-{e}^{-2st}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{-st})^{2}}=-{e}^{2st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t{e}^{st}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-t{e}^{-st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(-{e}^{-2st})(t{e}^{st})+(-{e}^{2st})(-t{e}^{-st}) \\  & =t{e}^{st}-t{e}^{-st} \\  & =t({e}^{st}-{e}^{-st}).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy-2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =({s}^{3}-t)^{2}={s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(s{t}^{2})({s}^{3}-t)-2=2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2+t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =s{e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2+t{e}^{s})(0)+(s{e}^{s})({e}^{s}) \\  & =s{e}^{2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})}=-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2ts, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}})\cdot 2ts+(-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}))\cdot (\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}})+(4)\cdot 2s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-4s+8s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}+4s \\  & =\frac{2(1+2{s}^{2})}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=xz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2s{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =s{e}^{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(ts{e}^{t+s})\cdot 0+(2t{e}^{s})\cdot s{e}^{t}+(2s{e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{s} \\  & =2ts{e}^{t+s}+2s{e}^{t+s} \\  & =2s(t+1){e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(3)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-2t)+(1)\cdot 0 \\  & =4t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} 
= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =[-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot 1+[-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})-t{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}) \\  & =-(1+t){e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2,$ where $x = s\cos{t}$ and $y = t\sin{s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(\operatorname{sin}⁡s) \\  & =-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t{sin}^{2}⁡s \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the identity $\sin 2t = 2\sin t\cos t$ in the above simplification.

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y,z) = e^{xy + z},$ where $x = s + t,$ $y = s-t$ and $z = -s^2.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059013/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{xy+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(s-t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(s+t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}={e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 1+(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot (-1)+{e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 0 \\  & =(s-t-s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}} \\  & =-2t{e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
